note.text: Shareholders hold ownership interests, while directors oversee a company and managers carry out delegated operations. Their roles can overlap but are not identical. Pooling equity can support expansion, while administration, reporting and conflicts of interest create costs. A private-company model restricts transfers or access to investors; a company offering securities to the public faces additional applicable requirements. Public offering is not the same as government ownership, and not every company is stock-exchange listed. Actual OHADA forms must be checked rather than importing foreign membership limits.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to distinguish ownership from management and evaluate benefits alongside governance costs. Builds on: separate legal identity, shares and continuity. Leads to: capital structure and the consequences of financing decisions.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: A fictional company’s managers propose buying machinery. Owners may expect returns, while directors must assess risks and oversight. A declared dividend can be allocated among identical shares, but owning shares does not guarantee a dividend every year. The illustration does not identify any real Cameroonian firm’s current ownership or performance.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Ask who owns, who supervises and who manages. Explain a potential benefit and its condition rather than asserting that incorporation automatically improves performance. Use only a dividend explicitly declared in the question; do not turn a model return into an investment promise.
